concepts.text:

concepts.title: Methods reveal different things.

terms.Electroencephalography: recording electrical activity at the scalp

points: Electroencephalography: recording electrical activity at the scalp
Functional imaging: estimating activity-related physiological changes
Lesion evidence: studying consequences of tissue damage
concepts.text:
Electroencephalography: recording electrical activity at the scalp. Functional imaging: estimating activity-related physiological changes. Lesion evidence: studying consequences of tissue damage.

Scalp electrical recordings have useful temporal resolution but limited source localization. Functional magnetic resonance imaging measures blood-oxygen-related changes rather than thoughts directly.

Lesions and carefully designed interventions can add causal evidence, but damage or stimulation can affect connected systems. Each method has practical and inferential limits.

title: A signal is a process, not a spark of personality
objective: Explain an action potential and distinguish electrical propagation from synaptic transmission.
hook: A signal is a process, not a spark of personality
story: A diagram at the café calls neurons tiny wires carrying thoughts. Sam asks what actually happens when a neural signal travels and reaches another cell.

concepts.title: Cells maintain an electrical difference.

terms.Neuron: a cell specialized for neural signalling
terms.Membrane potential: voltage difference across a cell membrane
terms.Ion channel: a membrane pathway for specific ions

points: Neuron: a cell specialized for neural signalling
Membrane potential: voltage difference across a cell membrane
Ion channel: a membrane pathway for specific ions
concepts.text:
Ion channel: a membrane pathway for specific ions.

Neurons maintain differences in charged particles across a membrane. Inputs can change the membrane potential. Dendrites and the cell body receive many inputs, while an axon can carry a propagated signal.

These are useful functional distinctions, with variation across neuron types. A single neuron is not a miniature thinking person.

visual.title: A simplified neuron
visual.caption: The diagram simplifies a diverse class of cells.

concepts.title: An action potential regenerates.

terms.Threshold: condition required to initiate a spike

points: Action potential: a brief propagated membrane-voltage change
Threshold: condition required to initiate a spike
Refractory period: interval limiting immediate refiring
concepts.text:
Action potential: a brief propagated membrane-voltage change. Refractory period: interval limiting immediate refiring.

When conditions reach threshold, voltage-sensitive channels support a rapid change in membrane potential. The process regenerates along the axon.

Individual spikes are broadly all-or-none. Information can depend on timing, firing rates and population patterns rather than a bigger spike meaning a stronger thought.

visual.title: A propagated event
visual.caption: A simplified action-potential sequence is not a psychological codebook.

concepts.title: The connection changes the next cell.

terms.Synapse: a junction for signalling between cells
terms.Neurotransmitter: chemical messenger released at a synapse
terms.Receptor: molecular target responsive to a messenger

points: Synapse: a junction for signalling between cells
Neurotransmitter: chemical messenger released at a synapse
Receptor: molecular target responsive to a messenger
concepts.text:
Synapse: a junction for signalling between cells. Neurotransmitter: chemical messenger released at a synapse. Receptor: molecular target responsive to a messenger.

At many synapses, an arriving signal triggers chemical release. A transmitter binds receptors that affect the receiving cell. Other synapses transmit electrically.

The effect depends on receptors, cell state and circuitry. A transmitter is not inherently a single emotion, and more of it does not imply more happiness.

visual.title: A chemical synapse
visual.caption: Receptor and circuit context determine the effect.

evidence:
Cellular physiology supports detailed mechanisms of signalling, while links from those mechanisms to complex behaviour require additional levels of evidence.

Electrical and chemical descriptions are complementary. Neither identifies a personality trait or emotion from one cell.

title: Networks work together
objective: Explain a brain function using interacting networks rather than a single-region personality label.
story: Leo says the left brain does logic and the right brain does creativity. Maya asks him to explain how Sam listens, remembers instructions and repairs a radio at the same time.

concepts.title: Anatomy gives landmarks, not isolated minds.

terms.Cerebral cortex: outer neural tissue of the cerebrum

points: Cerebral cortex: outer neural tissue of the cerebrum
Subcortical structure: structure beneath the cortex
Network: interacting set of connected regions
concepts.text:
Cerebral cortex: outer neural tissue of the cerebrum. Subcortical structure: structure beneath the cortex. Network: interacting set of connected regions.

Brain regions have different connections and contributions. Cortical and subcortical systems interact in perception, memory and action.

A task can involve several networks, and a region can contribute to several tasks. A labelled anatomical map is a starting point for understanding these interactions.

visual.title: Several contributions to a repair
visual.caption: The functions interact across connected systems.

concepts.title: Lateralization is not a personality test.
points: Lateralization: unequal contribution across hemispheres
Corpus callosum: major connection between the hemispheres
Functional specialization: relative contribution to a function
concepts.text:
Lateralization: unequal contribution across hemispheres. Corpus callosum: major connection between the hemispheres. Functional specialization: relative contribution to a function.

Some functions show hemispheric asymmetries. Many aspects of language are often left-lateralized, but variation and bilateral contributions matter.

Both hemispheres participate in complex reasoning and creative activity. Classifying a person as left-brained or right-brained is not supported by this anatomical distinction.

visual.title: A real distinction and an overreach
visual.caption: Hemispheric specialization does not divide people into thinking types.

concepts.title: Damage affects connected systems.

terms.Plasticity: experience-related change in a biological system
terms.Distributed processing: a function depends on interacting components

points: Plasticity: experience-related change in a biological system
Distributed processing: a function depends on interacting components
Compensation: another route helps maintain performance
concepts.text:
Plasticity: experience-related change in a biological system. Distributed processing: a function depends on interacting components. Compensation: another route helps maintain performance.

A lesion can disrupt local tissue and its connections. Changes in performance help investigate a system, but task demands and the extent of damage matter.

Recovery can involve practice, support and reorganization. It is not evidence that all regions are interchangeable or that every injury has the same prognosis.

visual.title: Interpret a lesion finding
visual.caption: A lesion supports a bounded system-level inference.

evidence:
Neuroscience combines anatomy, task measures and interventions to examine functional organization. Region labels alone cannot establish a psychological explanation.

The café repair is not a localization experiment. Brain-based personality quizzes need independent validation rather than anatomical metaphors.

concepts.title: Acute responses can support action.

terms.Stressor: a demand or threat capable of eliciting a response
terms.Stress response: coordinated response to a perceived demand
terms.Acute stress: a response over a relatively short period

points: Stressor: a demand or threat capable of eliciting a response
Stress response: coordinated response to a perceived demand
Acute stress: a response over a relatively short period
concepts.text:
Stressor: a demand or threat capable of eliciting a response. Stress response: coordinated response to a perceived demand. Acute stress: a response over a relatively short period.

Stress responses can mobilize attention and resources for immediate demands. Whether a response helps depends on the task, its intensity and the available resources.

A useful short-term response is not evidence that prolonged strain is harmless. Likewise, a long-term risk association does not mean every alarm response causes damage.

points: Hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: linked hormonal stress-regulation pathway

title: Sleep has timing and structure
objective: Distinguish circadian timing, sleep pressure and sleep stages in a practical sleep claim.
story: Pat feels sleepy late at night after a long day. Jo, working a shifted schedule, feels alert then but sleepy in the morning. Leo says both should simply decide to sleep at the same time.

concepts.title: Two processes shape sleep timing.

terms.Sleep pressure: need for sleep increasing with sustained wakefulness
terms.Entrainment: alignment of a rhythm to external timing cues

points: Circadian rhythm: approximately daily biological cycle
Sleep pressure: need for sleep increasing with sustained wakefulness
Entrainment: alignment of a rhythm to external timing cues
concepts.text:
Circadian rhythm: approximately daily biological cycle. Sleep pressure: need for sleep increasing with sustained wakefulness. Entrainment: alignment of a rhythm to external timing cues.

Sleep timing reflects both accumulated wakefulness and circadian regulation. Light is an important timing cue, alongside behaviour and social schedules.

Feeling alert does not necessarily mean a person is fully rested. Shift schedules can place biological timing and required activity in conflict.

visual.title: Different processes
visual.caption: The processes interact; this is a conceptual model, not a personal sleep score.

concepts.title: Sleep is not one uniform state.

terms.Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stages without rapid eye movements
terms.Rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stage with characteristic eye movements
terms.Sleep architecture: organization of sleep stages across time

points: Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stages without rapid eye movements
Rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stage with characteristic eye movements
Sleep architecture: organization of sleep stages across time
concepts.text:
Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stages without rapid eye movements. Rapid-eye-movement sleep: sleep stage with characteristic eye movements. Sleep architecture: organization of sleep stages across time.

Sleep cycles through stages identified using physiological measures. Stages differ in features such as brain activity, muscle tone and eye movements.

Sleep supports several functions, including aspects of memory and regulation. Dreams are not restricted to one simple function, and a stage label is not a unique psychological meaning.

concepts.title: A tracker is an estimate.

terms.Sleep opportunity: time and conditions available for sleeping
terms.Measurement validity: whether a measure supports its intended use

points: Sleep opportunity: time and conditions available for sleeping
Sleep deprivation: insufficient sleep relative to need
Measurement validity: whether a measure supports its intended use
concepts.text:
Sleep opportunity: time and conditions available for sleeping. Measurement validity: whether a measure supports its intended use.

Consumer devices infer sleep from limited signals; their estimates are not equivalent to a complete clinical sleep study. Judge a device against validation for its claimed use.

Persistent sleep difficulties, breathing concerns or excessive sleepiness warrant appropriate care. Do not alter medication or undertake sleep deprivation as course practice.

title: Genes act in developing systems
objective: Interpret heritability without treating a genetic association as individual destiny.
story: A visitor advertises a gene test for motivation. Leo says a high heritability estimate means a trait cannot change. Sam asks what the estimate describes and whether it explains an individual.

concepts.title: Genes are part of a process.

terms.Gene: a DNA sequence involved in biological function

points: Gene: a DNA sequence involved in biological function
Genotype: genetic constitution at relevant sites
Phenotype: an observed characteristic
concepts.text:
Gene: a DNA sequence involved in biological function. Genotype: genetic constitution at relevant sites.

Genes contribute through biological processes in developing environments. Complex psychological traits usually involve many variants with small, context-dependent associations.

A genetic association is not a single-purpose instruction for a behaviour. The phenotype depends on development, measurement and circumstances.

visual.title: Several levels between DNA and behaviour
visual.caption: A complex behaviour is not directly encoded as a single fixed instruction.

concepts.title: Heritability describes variation in a population.

terms.Heritability: proportion of observed variation attributed to genetic differences under a model
terms.Gene–environment correlation: genetic differences associated with environmental exposure

points: Heritability: proportion of observed variation attributed to genetic differences under a model
Gene–environment interaction: genetic effects vary across environments
Gene–environment correlation: genetic differences associated with environmental exposure
concepts.text:
Gene–environment interaction: genetic effects vary across environments. Gene–environment correlation: genetic differences associated with environmental exposure.

Heritability concerns differences within a specified population and range of environments. It does not state what percentage of one person’s trait is genetic.

A high estimate does not imply that environmental changes are ineffective. Estimates can change when conditions or measurement change.

visual.title: Population and individual
visual.caption: A variance estimate does not divide an individual into genetic and environmental parts.

concepts.title: Prediction and explanation differ.

terms.Polygenic score: weighted summary of many genetic associations

points: Polygenic score: weighted summary of many genetic associations
Population transfer: performance in a different population
Association: statistical relationship without automatic causation
concepts.text:
Polygenic score: weighted summary of many genetic associations. Population transfer: performance in a different population. Association: statistical relationship without automatic causation.

A genetic score’s predictive value depends on the outcome, sample and reference data. Performance can fall in populations unlike the study group.

Prediction does not identify a modifiable mechanism or justify ranking someone’s worth. Privacy and informed consent matter for genetic information.

visual.title: Evaluate a genetic product
visual.caption: A marketed score needs evidence for its intended practical use.

evidence:
Genetically informative studies rely on design assumptions and measured environments. Association studies need replication and careful attention to population structure.

An introductory example cannot validate a genetic product or establish an individual prognosis.

options: A fixed percentage of one person’s trait.
Variation in a population under specified conditions.
How much a trait can never change.
feedback: The estimate is about population variation, not a personal decomposition.
Population, environment range, measure and model define its interpretation.
Heritability and modifiability are different questions.

Why may a polygenic score transfer poorly?

Its associations and reference data may not match the new population or environment.

title: Experience changes systems, within limits
objective: Distinguish task-specific plasticity from a claim of general brain improvement.
story: After weeks of practice, Sam identifies familiar radio faults faster. A training app calls this proof of a stronger brain. Maya asks whether the improvement transfers to an unfamiliar task.

concepts.title: Plasticity is change, not a promise.

terms.Neuroplasticity: change in neural organization or function
terms.Synaptic plasticity: change in the effectiveness of connections

points: Neuroplasticity: change in neural organization or function
Experience-dependent change: change associated with particular experience
Synaptic plasticity: change in the effectiveness of connections
concepts.text:
Neuroplasticity: change in neural organization or function. Experience-dependent change: change associated with particular experience. Synaptic plasticity: change in the effectiveness of connections.

Nervous systems change with development, experience, injury and learning. Plasticity includes several mechanisms and timescales.

Calling an activity plasticity does not tell us whether a change is beneficial or durable. The effect must be measured against a specific outcome.

concepts.title: Practice can improve a specific task.

terms.Near transfer: benefit on a closely related task
terms.Far transfer: benefit on a substantially different task
terms.Active control: comparison with a credible alternative activity

points: Near transfer: benefit on a closely related task
Far transfer: benefit on a substantially different task
Active control: comparison with a credible alternative activity
concepts.text:
Near transfer: benefit on a closely related task. Far transfer: benefit on a substantially different task. Active control: comparison with a credible alternative activity.

Sam may learn the regularities of familiar repairs. That is useful even if general memory does not change.

To test a broader benefit, compare suitable groups on untrained outcomes, account for expectations and assess persistence. A pre-to-post improvement without a comparison leaves practice and other explanations open.

Prognosis: anticipated course with uncertainty

title: Build a biological explanation carefully
objective: Combine neural, psychological and contextual evidence in a bounded practical recommendation.
story: The café considers a brain-based wellbeing workshop. Its advert combines genetic scores, hormone checks and a short training game. The team wants to distinguish credible concepts from unsupported product claims.

concepts.title: Connect levels without skipping steps.

terms.Reductionism: explaining a complex phenomenon only at a narrower level

points: Reductionism: explaining a complex phenomenon only at a narrower level
Multilevel explanation: linking relevant levels of analysis
Causal chain: specified sequence of influences
concepts.text:
Reductionism: explaining a complex phenomenon only at a narrower level. Multilevel explanation: linking relevant levels of analysis. Causal chain: specified sequence of influences.

A biological explanation can connect cells, circuits, behaviour and environment. Each link needs evidence rather than an attractive metaphor.

A brain correlate does not identify the only cause, and a social context is not biologically irrelevant. Ask how the proposed levels interact in the actual task.

visual.title: Link the explanation
visual.caption: A multilevel explanation tests links rather than merely listing levels.

concepts.title: Evaluate the intervention claim separately.

terms.Generalizability: applicability to other settings or populations
terms.Adverse effect: an unwanted consequence of an intervention

points: Efficacy: effect under specified study conditions
Generalizability: applicability to other settings or populations
Adverse effect: an unwanted consequence of an intervention
concepts.text:
Generalizability: applicability to other settings or populations. Adverse effect: an unwanted consequence of an intervention.

A product can use accurate neuroscience terms while making an untested practical claim. Check the comparison group, sample, outcome, follow-up and unwanted effects.

Ask whether the benefit matters in everyday life and whether the study tested the actual product. Biological plausibility is not a substitute for efficacy evidence.

visual.title: Read beyond the biological label
visual.caption: A plausible mechanism and an effective intervention are distinct claims.

concepts.title: Keep choices proportionate.

terms.Biological determinism: treating biology as a fixed inevitable cause

points: Informed consent: agreement based on relevant information
Biological determinism: treating biology as a fixed inevitable cause
Uncertainty: limits in what evidence establishes
concepts.text:
Informed consent: agreement based on relevant information. Biological determinism: treating biology as a fixed inevitable cause. Uncertainty: limits in what evidence establishes.

Use the evidence to ask better questions and improve accessible conditions. Avoid diagnosing, prescribing or interpreting another person’s private biological data.

Health decisions need qualified care and informed choice. If a claim exceeds the evidence, narrow it rather than replacing it with another certainty.

evidence:

The image proves the workshop treats a disorder.
A signal changed, but clinical benefit and transfer remain untested.
feedback: Environmental conditions can influence biological responses and behaviour.
The measurement is not evidence of clinical efficacy by itself.
This separates the measured change from the untested practical claim.
quiz.context: A small uncontrolled study finds a brain-signal difference after a workshop but measures no daily-life benefit.
quiz.reasoningPrompt: Explain your choice. Which evidence supports it, what alternative remains, and what would change your conclusion?
